maintopic: REPORTED SHELVING OF CANADIAN PROPOSAL FOR SUMMIT CONFERENCE
speechtext:
I think the hon. gentleman has brought two circumstances together. The request for a meeting of heads of government in Ottawa was to discuss the various matters that require to be considered in NATO to assure the maintenance and preservation of NATO.
The situation in recent months, indeed in the last several months, in NATO has not been such as to indicate evidence of that agreement or unity which one would hope would be characteristic of this great defensive organization, and the Canadian representative suggested a meeting of heads of government in Ottawa. subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON VISIT TO WASHINGTON

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON VISIT TO WASHINGTON
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Justice. Has the minister any information to give the house concerning his recent visit to Washington for negotiations between Canadian and United States representatives with respect to the development of the Columbia river?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulion (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON VISIT TO WASHINGTON
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. I have received communications from several members from British Columbia indicating their interest in this matter, so I prepared the following brief report.
The talks in Washington were extremely productive. They were scheduled for December 14 and 15 but were extended for another full day and lasted until 7 p.m. on Friday the 16th. As a result we were able to issue an official communique reporting that our consideration of various drafts of a treaty based on the principles of the progress report of September 28 had produced satisfactory progress toward agreement on a Anal text of a treaty.
As a matter of fact, agreement in principle for purposes of treaty drafting was recorded on all points of substance in connection with the operation of Canadian storages for downstream benefits in terms of power and flood control, and the relation thereto of non-treaty projects which may be developed in Canada. I am satisfied that an acceptable and advantageous result to Canada will ensue. Only one or two points of substance remain to be reduced to the form of agreement for treaty purposes, and these are not concerned with the agreed operation and returns for Canadian storages as such.
A further meeting of negotiators has been arranged for January 5 and 6, 1961, in Ottawa. On the basis of progress to date, I am satisfied that we can reach our Objective as negotiators, that is agreement on a treaty text, very early in the year.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Finance. Has the minister received a recent billet-doux from the premier of British Columbia with respect to the financing of the development of the Columbia river? If so, can he give the house any information as to its contents?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO LETTER FROM B.C. PREMIER
speechtext:
I have received a communication from the premier of British Columbia, although I do not know whether it would be accurately described as a billet-doux. It is a letter dated December 14, 1960, purporting to be a reply to the letter I wrote to him on December 6, which letter appears at pages 608 and 609 of Hansard of December 8. As Premier Bennett's letter is quite brief, Mr. Speaker, perhaps I might read it.
Dear Mr. Fleming:
This will acknowledge your letter of December 6 in reply to my letter to you of October 27.
The financial proposals put forward by the government of Canada for hydroelectric development of the Columbia river are, regrettably, unacceptable to British Columbia. In order that there will be no delay in carrying out the development, however, British Columbia is prepared to guarantee Canada that this government will fulfill the terms of the treaty which is negotiated with the government of the United States. In return, British Columbia would, of course, expect the government of Canada to guarantee that the obligations imposed on the United States government by terms of the treaty will be fulfilled.
Yours faithfully,
W.A.C. Bennett Premier
Concerning the second part of the hon. member's question, I would say that it is a matter of deep regret and disappointment that the premier of British Columbia has undertaken to reject out of hand the very generous, indeed extremely generous, offer
Inquiries of the Ministry made to him on behalf of the federal government in relation to the financing of the Columbia river development. In expressing this very keen regret I think I may be permitted to say that the rejection came so swiftly that one is driven to wonder whether the federal government's offer was fully considered or adequately understood.
In that regard, I may express further regret that the premier of British Columbia did not avail himself of the opportunity that was offered to him at the time he received my letter to discuss the matter with my colleague, the Minister of Justice, who was then in Victoria in consultation with ministers of the British Columbia government. I may add that if Premier Bennett is prepared to discuss this matter further I shall be happy to meet him at any time to discuss further the really very generous offer that has been put forward on behalf of the federal government.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO LETTER FROM B.C. PREMIER
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question. May I ask the Minister of Finance if this is another example of that new harmony which has been established with the provincial governments?

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO LETTER FROM B.C. PREMIER

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR ELIMINATION OF EXCISE TAX
speechtext:
The votes requested in these supplementary estimates are in addition to those provided under the departmental votes for the current fiscal year. These additional amounts will enable the department to undertake work projects apart from those already carried out or yet to be performed under the regular construction program for 1960-61, and will provide additional employment on various Indian reserves across Canada.
Included in the total estimate is an amount of $250,000, which will provide funds to finance a departmental program of winter works for Indians on various reserves. The purpose of this program is to assist those bands which have insufficient funds to participate in the winter works incentive program sponsored by the Department of Labour.
It should be made clear that these items have no connection whatever with the Department of Labour program for which funds are being requested under item 592 of the supple-mentaries. I should add, however, that Indian bands that have funds at their disposal are applying for consideration under the Department of Labour winter works incentive program and as of December 9 some 32 projects were approved for an amount of $189,950. It is our estimate that these projects will supply 550 Indians with work.
However, to return to the supplementary estimates of my own department, may I say this. The $250,000 of which I spoke a moment ago is to be found in four estimates. In this regard I may say that I can see where there might have been a little bit of confusion because of these estimates having been split into four separate parcels. However, I can assure hon. members that this was not the doing of my department or my officials but rather was the course insisted upon by the treasury board.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR ELIMINATION OF EXCISE TAX
speechtext: Confusion in the board?

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR ELIMINATION OF EXCISE TAX
speechtext:
I agree that it might have been a little bit clearer had we not been required to put in four estimates, but since they perhaps fall into four categories they felt that it was proper that the apportionment should fall into those categories. Under the first item, 578, Indian agencies, operation and

maintenance, the amount is $50,000. Under the next item, item 579, it is $150,000; under item 580 it is $35,000 and under item 581 it is $15,000 which brings the total tor this project to $250,000. Then there is a total of $5,000 in the next item, 582, which is also entirely for labour.
The projects to be undertaken under these items are of the type in which the maximum amount of day labour will be used, and Indians to be employed will be paid at rates prevailing in their areas.
As of December 13 some 124 projects had been approved. These projects we expect will call for an expenditure of $235,675. These projects cover such things as brushing and clearing roadways, housing, sites, school playgrounds, repairs to existing roads where possible, repairs to water supply systems, cutting fuel wood for destitute Indians and other work. Additional projects will be dealt with as applications are received from the field offices. It is estimated that approximately 1,430 Indians, mainly heads of families, will be employed on the 124 projects.
The remaining amount of this further supplementary estimate which will be in the amount of $1,049,500 is to cover works in addition to or to accelerate projects provided for in the main estimates of the current fiscal year. These additional works will provide for an additional amount of employment in areas where they are to be executed, not only for Indians but for non-Indians as well.
I think the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, who is momentarily absent from the chamber, asked some questions with reference to works which had been undertaken or were about to be undertaken in his area.

I should like the minister to bring us up to date on this matter. Would he tell us whether this committee still exists and is still in operation? The minister will remember that at one stage it was suggested that consideration should be given to handing over to the federation some of the vessels of Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships and I know that at the time the answer was that they were not suitable. Nevertheless, they operated between ports of the maritime provinces, the port of Montreal and the West Indies Federation over a period of many years and carried much of the trade between our two countries. In the circumstances it was natural that we should ask why these ships were not being used.
I do not know that we have had a satisfactory answer. Perhaps now, in the light of what has transpired and in view of the progress that has been made with the construction of these ships, it is possible to give a more complete answer to that question. External Affairs

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it was at the commonwealth trade and economic conference at Montreal in the autumn of 1958 that those of us who were there representing the Canadian government announced a program of $10 million of assistance to the new federation of the West Indies. It was intended that this program would be spread over a five-year period. What elements should enter into the program were, of course, to be a matter for discussion between the representatives of the government of Canada and the representatives of the federation. Very early the representatives of the federation asked for a ship.
Let me say at once that this was not intended to be a ship operating between Canada and the West Indies. That is why, as the hon. member for Laurier has indicated, it was stated at the time that the type of ships that were in the fleet of the Canadian National West Indies steamship service were not regarded by the West Indies Federation representatives as suitable.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I just say a word there? The minister is aware that these ships in the Canadian National West Indies steamship fleet operated between the various islands now forming part of the federation today.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
What was sought by the representatives of the federation was a ship for interisland shipping purposes. The islands of the federation are scattered over 2,000 miles in the Atlantic ocean, and it was thought a ship, and then later a second ship, would be of great benefit in welding these scattered islands together with some sense of common interest. The provision of one ship for interisland service was, therefore, approved.
Soon after a request was made for a second ship, and that request was also approved. The letting of the contracts for this purpose was approved by cabinet in October, 1959. The contract for the construction of one ship was awarded to Port Weller Dry Dock Limited, Port Weller, Ontario, and the other to Canadian Vickers Limited, Montreal. The ships are identical. Each will have a cargo capacity of 80,000 cubic feet. There will be accommodation for 50 cabin passengers and 200 deck passengers on each ship. Originally it appeared that the cost of the two ships would amount to as much as $7.5 million.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Each?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, in aggregate. Further discussions have taken place from time to time and changes have been made in the specifications. The present estimate is that the two ships will cost in aggregate $6


million. We had, as a government, some concern over so much of the aid program going into the provision of the two ships, at a time when it appeared that the cost of the two would amount to the larger figure I mentioned, the $7.5 million. We had hoped that some of the original $10 million program would be available for other purposes. The scaling down of the cost of these ships from the estimated $7.5 million to $6 million in aggregate opened the way for the provision of some other elements in the aid program. These will be coming forward, it is expected, in the next fiscal year.
Now, less progress was made last year, that is in the last fiscal year, on the construction of these ships than had been expected, and there was some money left in the vote for this purpose at the end of the year. In the main estimates for the present fiscal year, 1960-61, there was a total amount provided in item 78 of $4,510,000 for this West Indies assistance program. Hon. members will recall having approved that vote, and that it included provision for the ships.
In the meantime the pace of progress has quickened, and by the provision of this proposed additional sum in the present supplementary estimates, item No. 585, it will be possible to accelerate substantially the construction of these two ships. This sum of $750,000 will be required to carry forward the construction of these ships at this accelerated rate to March 31.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I have a few further details? Would the minister tell the committee when the contract was awarded for the first ship and for the second ship, or were both awarded at the same time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My note is that it was on October 26 that the letting of contracts for both ships was approved.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What transpired between the year 1958, the time when the first ship was approved, and October 26, 1959? More than a year elapsed before the contract was awarded. What was the reason for the delay?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Discussions commenced, Mr. Chairman, in the winter of 195859, and it was in March, 1959 that approval was given on behalf of the Canadian government to the provision of the two ships. Then there were further discussions between the representatives of Canada and the federation with a view to settling the specifications of the ships. This required some considerable time. On the one hand the federation representatives were asking for certain things in the ships, and on the other the concern of the Canadian government was that the utmost value should be obtained from the

grants that were being made in terms of benefit in the construction of the ships, and there were extended discussions about the specifications of the two vessels.
Are both ships alike?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, my information is that they are identical.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Will they be assigned exclusively to interisland transportation and not between the federation and Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am informed that is the intention of the government of the federation.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The cost of the ships, according to the minister, will run now to about $6 million, and we voted in the main estimates about $4,800,000. There is another $750,000 here-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Well, $4,510,000, then, and now another $750,000, making a total of $5,200,000-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is expected that the ships will be completed in June of next year.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: In June, 1961?

speechtext:
That question has nothing to do with the item under review here at all. However, that matter is not within the scope of the present item which is a matter of aid, according

Supply-External Affairs to the form of aid or assistance requested by the federation of the West Indies.

All I want to speak on is the point of order. I aim glad the minister has told us that he does not know the answer to what I asked him. However, the minister might have saved himself from raising a long point of order because we are asked to pay for some new boats while we may very well realize, within a limited number of months, that we have a large number of vessels for that purpose.

586.	Contribution towards the administrative expenses of the freedom-from-hunger campaign of the Food and Agriculture Organization, $23,000.
Can the minister explain this item? I do not notice an item in the blue book under this heading.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Item 586, which is one for $23,000, is for a contribution on a once and for all basis, not a continuing form of contribution, toward the administrative expenses of a campaign organized by the Food and Agriculture Organization and known as the freedom from hunger campaign. This matter dates from October, 1959 when, at the tenth conference of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations held at Rome authorization was given to the director general to proceed with the development of a five-year campaign, namely the freedom from hunger campaign, designed to speed up production in food deficient countries. The campaign has developed from that genesis. In July, 1960 the campaign was officially opened at Rome with messages of support from many countries. The director general of the F.A.O. formally asked the Canadian government as well as governments of other countries to provide a second grant toward the administrative expenses of the campaign and to permit the establishment of a local committee.
Canada's share has been worked out on the basis of the same percentage as applies to Canada's share of the United Nations budget, namely 3.11 per cent. The $23,000 represents Canada's share on that percentage basis. The United Kingdom has followed the same course, as also has the Netherlands government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is a Canadian committee but this vote has nothing to do with the Canadian committee. This vote

provides Canada's share of the campaign expenses of the committee set up at Rome.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Of course the food bank is something that must be taken into account in any plans that are concerted in this respect. However, the primary purpose of this present campaign is to do what may be possible to increase the production of food in food deficient countries.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman. I shall be glad to give that information. This present estimate is an unusual item. Normally, or at least in recent years, the house has voted $1,500,000 for this contingency purpose in the main estimates. The amount is often exceeded but the expenditure charged against the item at no time is permitted to exceed that sum. However, as amounts are paid out of the fund with authorization they are sometimes replaced as the result of the enactment subsequently of supplementary estimates.
In seven of the last eight years the amount of the vote has been $1,500,000. In the year 1955-56 it was $1 million, but $1,500,000 has become a sort of standard amount. The reason for asking for the additional sum at this time is in order to facilitate the acceleration of works programs; it is entirely intended for acceleration. The sum committed already against this item exceeds $1.3 million and it is expected that in order to take care of the acceleration of programs under a number of items it may be necessary to call on this sum, to have it available so that the utmost in work creation can be accomplished with respect to programs of construction and other work creating projects.
Does this mean that the minister or his colleagues in the departments responsible for construction underestimated the speed with which they could carry on their operations?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No; not if the hon. member is speaking now of the time when the main estimates for the present fiscal year 1960-61 were compiled in the autumn of 1959 and tabled in the house in 1960. But as hon. members are aware, a definite effort has been made to expedite and accelerate programs of construction in various departments that provide work creating opportunities during this present winter. In the course of that acceleration which was applied in various departments the need for a contingency item naturally grows.

In a budget of the size of Canada's it has been found that even exercising the utmost ingenuity in the autumn of the year in the preparation of the estimates for the ensuing fiscal year it is not possible to anticipate everything that may happen during the course of that fiscal year.

been any pretence or any attempt to create an impression that item 590 is a part of the winter works program in the sense in which that term is generally used.
To deal with the question the hon. member for Essex East posed to me, it is true that there has been a disturbing number of irregularities brought to light in connection with the administration of bankrupt estates. This investigation, which has been under way for a good many months, has now resulted in establishing that there have been many irregularities which we are now proceeding to deal with on an individual basis in so far as prosecutions are concerned, and to regularize the individual estates.
I am not yet in a position to indicate what changes, if any, in the bankruptcy law will be made. I hope to be in a position to make a more definite forecast by the time the main estimates for 1961-62 are reached. What we have been doing so far has been to invite representations and suggestions from responsible organizations in this field indicating their views as to how the act might be amended so as to make better control of the administration of the estates possible than apparently has been the situation up to now. What we have before us now does suggest that the administration by individual trustees has been such that the inference can be drawn that there is a lack of supervision and control. This, in my view, and in a large measure, is inherent in the system envisaged by the act itself.
We are studying the matter on our own in order to see what changes could be made in the legislation so as to enable a better system of trusts to be devised. At the same time we are asking for representations by trust company associations and similar organizations which we are certain will be extremely helpful to us in arriving at our own conclusions as to what legislation should be recommended.
I am sorry that I cannot go further than that at the present time. If I were to attempl any definite forecast of what might be introduced by way of legislative changes I might find that I was obliged to change my mind between now and the time when the legislation was introduced and I should not like to be open to the charge by the hon. gentlemen of having been inaccurate with respect to the forecast that I made.

Under this item I should like to ask one question which is related to the administration of the Bankruptcy Act, and it is not a product of my imagination. It springs from the harsh reality of trusting employees and businessmen who are suffering from the administration of a United States lumber company in my district which

has gone into liquidation. The question I wish to ask is this. Have disgruntled or suspicious creditors with respect to a voluntary liquidation the right under the Bankruptcy Act to lay their complaints before the superintendent of bankruptcy and to seek an investigation of these circumstances?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I shall be obliged to answer this question without the benefit of advice of my legal officers who are not here. It would be my understanding, however-and this is subject to correction-that voluntary liquidation would not be within the jurisdiction of the superintendent of bankruptcy or of parliament under the Bankruptcy Act but that liquidations are matters of provincial concern, with this exception. I know that certain clearances under the Income Tax Act are required before the affairs of a company can be wound up. However, I am not aware that there is anything in connection with voluntary liquidation which would come under the ambit of the bankruptcy legislation.
I understand that my hon. friend has forwarded certain representations in connection with the case to which he referred. I know that a check was made of my files and of those of the superintendent of bankruptcy in order to ascertain whether we have, in fact, received those representations. Up to the present time I am advised that we have not been able to locate them. It may be that the Chirstmas mail rush has delayed their receipt.
I want to inform the minister that I wrote a letter on December 9. I was advised by the superintendent of bankruptcy this afternoon that they had found my letter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member's information is a little bit later than mine.

From the minister's answer to a question by the hon. member for Essex East I understood that these inquiries have been going on for many months. I wonder whether the minister could advise the committee as to when these investigations started. Was it possible to foresee these investigations and the cost of them when the main estimates were brought down in the spring.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No. It was not possible to forecast it at that time. Up until just a few months ago we had thought that we might be able, by the appointment of a single prosecutor, to dispose of all the cases. It was not until he began to get into the details of what would be necessary and to find that as the R.C.M.P. took possession of the files there were so many hundreds of estates involved and which, by virtue of the fact that the files were seized
Supply-Justice
and taken in possession of the police, were therefore in a position in which no one could deal with them from the point of view of administering those estates. As I say, it therefore became necessary to consider what to do in that regard.
It became obvious that, in addition to the legal services of a prosecutor, we would require the services of accountants to go through the files and find out just exactly what had been done, what was the nature of any defalcations and also to find out what was the position of the bankrupt estates themselves so that we could make some assessment as to how we were going to be able to deal with them and whether it was feasible to appoint a new trustee to carry on the administration of those estates. That situation and the complexity of the situation even arising out of the affairs of a single trustee in bankruptcy were not revealed until the main estimates for the current year had been prepared.
The first part of the investigation was carried on by the R.C.M.P.?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is correct.
It was only after inquiry by the R.C.M.P. that the situation came to light?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. An agent had arranged to take out the files and lay charges and it was when that stage of the investigation was arrived at that we saw for the first time the complex nature of the operation that was necessary to sort this whole thing out.

There is a question that was not answered by the Minister of Justice and it is this. Is this amount asked for here in this item of $50,000 the same amount that was asked by the Minister of Finance under item 587? We were told that in the $1,500,000 under item 587 there was $50,000 for the Bankruptcy Act administration. Is that the same amount? Is that to be reimbursement or what is it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think there must be a misunderstanding there. This item of $50,000 stands on its own feet. We do not look to the $1,500,000 item in vote 587 for any part of it.
The Minister of Finance told us that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think my hon. friend must inadvertently have misunderstood what the Minister of Finance said. I know that my colleague the Minister of Finance has too clear an understanding of these matters for anything he has said to be really capable on analysis of creating that impression.

I can tell you that his lucidity in this matter was not great.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In any event this item is asked for by way of a request to parliament to authorize us to spend up to $50,000 for the purpose of prosecutions and completion of investigations now under way.

I think the Minister of Finance should be called back into this chamber in order to clear up this matter. I asked the Minister of Finance this specific question: Is the $50,000 now being asked for under item 590 to be used to reimburse the miscellaneous and unforeseen item and the minister said yes. That statement will be found in Hansard.
There is no doubt about that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Perhaps you might permit me, Mr. Chairman, to clear up the matter. The situation is this. In the commitments on the main item, the unforeseen item of $1,500,000, a commitment of $50,000 was made. That commitment is now to be reimbursed to that fund from item 590 which the committee is being asked to vote.
That is what the Minister of Finance said.
That is not what the Minister of Justice said. The Minister of Justice has said just the opposite.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I should say that it does not form any part of the $1,500,000 which parliament was asked to vote and has voted in item 587.
It goes back into the original item.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It goes back into the main unforeseen item voted by parliament at the last session.

That matter is clear now. The Minister of Finance and the Minister of Justice cannot both be right. The Minister of Justice is here. He can defend himself now in the light of the statement made by the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance. If he makes a defence that will appeal to all of us, we will be on his side. But obviously he has taken a position that is absolutely contrary to that statement by the Minister of Finance. What the parliamentary secretary has just now said confirms that view.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This statement, of course, reveals the extent of the misunderstanding on the part of my friend. The question which he asked and the one which I answered was whether item 590 forms part of item 587 and the answer I gave was no, that it did not form part of item 587, and that it stands

on its own feet. That answer is perfectly consistent with the situation as outlined by the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance who has just repeated what I now understand to have been the explanation previously given by this minister, namely that in the main estimates there was an item for $1,500,000 against which a commitment was made for the purpose of the Bankruptcy Act administration of $50,000.
We are now seeking parliamentary authority for an item under our supplementary estimates of $50,000 with which to reimburse that fund for which parliamentary authority was given on the earlier occasion. That fund is not the same; that earlier $1.5 million contingency item is not the same as the $1.5 million contained in item 587, so there is no inconsistency whatever between the explanations.

Up to now I fail to understand that distinction. We were told just a moment ago by the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance that in the main estimates of $1,500,000 there were $50,000 for the Bankruptcy Act administration.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is not correct. I would like my hon. friend to have a proper understanding of this contingency item. There was an item of $1,500,000 in the main estimates to cover unforeseen contingencies. There was an encumbrance against that item of $50,000 because we had already to start paying out these special amounts to our special prosecutor and investigator. So there was an encumbrance of $50,000 against that $1.5 million contingency item which was authorized in the main estimates. We are now including item 590 in the supplementary estimates to obtain parliamentary approval under the Bankruptcy Act administration to reimburse that $50,000.

The question is-I want to take the word of the Minister of Justice for it__the Minister of Justice said that this investigation was not foreseen when the main estimates were compiled. How is it, with this unforeseen event, that there is an item of $50,000 for the Bankruptcy Act administration?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
At the time of the main estimates there was no such item. What happened was that the main estimates were prepared, as is the usual custom, with a $1.5 million fund out of the Department of Finance to cover unforeseen contingencies.
Those main estimates were approved. Since the time of the passage of the main estimates a contingency has arisen, namely we went to treasury board and said, "We are faced with this very complicated investigation; we

are going to have to hire at least a lawyer and an accountant, and possibly another auditor; this will cost money, and we have no provision in our estimates for that money". We were told, "We will give you a commitment of $50,000 from the contingency fund that parliament has already voted in the main estimates; in other words, we will commit $50,000 to meet the contingency that has now arisen and in the supplementary estimates it will be included in an item under Bankruptcy Act administration to reimburse that fund in the amount of $50,000."
The specific contingency was not foreseen at the time of the main estimates. What was foreseen was the possibility of contingencies arising, so $1.5 million was authorized by parliament for that purpose. Now the specific contingency has arisen. There was a commitment against that fund and item 590 is for the purpose of reimbursing that fund that was voted in the main estimates.
Could we be advised how much of that $50,000 has already been spent.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am sorry; I do not have that information. I would have to get a good many particulars from the department to see what bills had been rendered and paid so far, and what telegraph and telephone bills have been rendered and paid so far in order to answer that question. Roughly speaking, we have estimated that one half of it will be required by the end of the present fiscal year to cover the costs of expert accounting and auditing services, and a further $25,000- or the other half-for legal expenses and fees.

As this money is in the main to pay for certain investigations and prosecutions as outlined by the minister, I would like to ask him a question on one phase that I think is of importance and has rather intrigued me for some time. Has there by any possibility been any investigation into some individuals in Canada-and I know of some in British Columbia-who seem to be making a practice of going bankrupt, forming new companies and then, by devious means, transferring the business or the assets of the previous company in which they went into bankruptcy? I am afraid this is becoming a practice by certain individuals. I would like to know whether any part of the investigation has been into this practice, and whether any prosecutions are contemplated or have been carried out in that line.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No irregularities involving criminal prosecutions against trustees have come to light in British Columbia. However, the situation that has been disclosed as a result of the investigations we have made have, as I say, suggested to us that there is
Supply-J ustice
a certain lack of control with respect to the administration of estates by trustees generally. That is to say, there is an inability on our part to supervise as closely and as effectively as we would like the activities of individual trustees in connection with the administration of bankrupt estates. It is that aspect of it which we are studying in connection with the legislation generally.
It may be that there are cases in other parts of the country where there has been some laxity, but all I can say is that up to the present time no case has been drawn to our attention, either officially or unofficially, which suggests that there is a situation which would warrant criminal prosecution. But the general control of bankruptcy and the situation regarding the discharge of bankrupts may well be covered and, I hope, improved as a result of any legislative changes that we might introduce.

Perhaps I could add one word. If that phase has not been covered in the investigations already underway I would very sincerely like to ask the Minister of Justice to extend his investigation into what I am afraid is becoming too much a common practice in Canada by certain individuals; that is, going into bankruptcy and taking advantage of their own bankruptcy through the incorporation of new companies, and carrying on business as though they had never gone into bankruptcy.
I think a person who does a thing like that is just as much a criminal as a person who goes in with a gun and holds up a store or a bank. If they are allowed-as I am afraid they are now-to get away with that kind of legal robbery I think the minister should have that matter very thoroughly investigated and should bring in, when he brings in other changes to the Bankruptcy Act, a protection whereby those who pull that kind of stunt cannot carry on in business until they have made good the bankruptcy of their previous company in the same business.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If my hon. friend would bring to our attention any cases where he thinks there has been an abuse of the bankruptcy laws or the procedures of the courts under the Bankruptcy Act, we would be very glad indeed to investigate.
If they can do it inside the law now the law should be changed so they cannot do it again.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This is precisely the point I was trying to meet earlier, that our investigation has disclosed a situation which to us indicates there should be a revision of the Bankruptcy Act. I would hope that when that

Supply-Justice
revision is made it will enable us to deal with the type of case to which I believe my hon. friend is referring.
However, I must say that at the present time the discharge of a bankrupt is dependent upon an order of the court. If the bankrupt is able to satisfy the court that he has discharged the conditions of his bankruptcy, with the consent of creditors, and the report of the trustee is obtained, then the bankrupt may be discharged and he is free to re-enter businesss.
To start business the next day.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If it is a case in which discharges are given too readily and the conditions that must be met can properly be made more onerous-these are the things we will be looking at in connection with the study of the legislation.
Can the minister tell the committee the number of bankruptcies in Canada last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, I do not have that information before me, Mr. Chairman.
I know there are well over 1,000 a year.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Oh, yes.
Has there been an investigation as to the reasons why so many businesses go into bankruptcy each year? Has there been an investigation that would reveal the main and secondary reasons?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Of course, Mr. Chairman, my department is not concerned with the economic causes of bankruptcy but with the bankruptcy laws under which bankrupt estates are administered and under which bankrupts are required to make good on what they can of their liabilities and on their discharges. We do not conduct any economic survey. These investigations have not primarily been concerned with the economic factors underlying bankruptcies.
I should also say that this investigation was not started because of any concern over an increase in the number of bankruptcies but because of a growing indication as it came to our attention of irregularities in connection with the administration of bankrupt estates. It was with that aspect alone that this investigation was concerned.

I agree with the minister but does he not think that it would be a good idea to investigate in co-operation with the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Trade and Commerce the reasons for so many bankruptcies? Many bankruptcies occur because of robbery and some because of false

methods of accounting. The Minister of Justice might be interested in investigating the effect of trading stamps on small businesses. Recently the supreme court declared that trading stamps are legal. Perhaps many people patronize larger stores because trading stamps are not available in smaller stores. This may contribute to the bankruptcy of some firms. Perhaps it would be a good idea for the Minister of Justice to amend the Criminal Code in order to declare trading stamps illegal. The minister should take these things into consideration because of the advisability of co-operating with his colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce in investigating why so many bankruptcies occur in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I can only assure my hon. friend that the irregularities we are investigating-and our investigation is confined to that-are not of recent origin. Many of them go back over many years to the period before 1957 and were committed on the part of persons who received their appointment before 1957. We have nothing new about the situation we are investigating, only we are the ones who have brought it to a head.
Item agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
before you proceed to the other items I wonder if I might ask you to revert to item No. 587. It has been brought to my attention that an answer I gave to a question that was put to me was based on a quite wrong premise. To that extent I wish to put the record right and apologize for my misunderstanding of the basis of the question. May I have leave to revert to that item?
Mr. Chairman, I think we might give the minister that privilege without even reverting to the item. The hon. gentleman does not want to become unstuck again.
Agreed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Thank you very much. I think it was the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate who asked me about the total of the amount of the reimbursement. I gave the figure $117,000. The basis of that figure is items that have been reimbursed. In other words, there has been some reimbursement as a result of votes in the supplementaries earlier in the year.
It is not the fact that $117,000 is the amount in these present supplementaries that is to be reimbursed. The amount is much larger. I can give that figure to the committee. But in the misunderstanding I had about the basis of the question and my participation

in it I wish to express my apologies to the committee because we are dealing in the one case with a reimbursement made hitherto and in the other case-and I have been told this is the basis of the question-with the amount in these present supplementaries that will be reimbursable when the items are passed.

As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, I was extremely incredulous that the minister would have committed such a large part of his $1.5 million and would be asking us to vote to other departments only $117,000 to pay him back. I thought it was shockingly bad business but the minister was so emphatic about it that I supposed he must have been right. Perhaps the minister wants to do the addition quite carefully and it may be rather complicated but I wonder if before the supplementaries are completely passed the minister would give us the correct figure, the global figure, as it were.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can do it now, Mr. Chairman.
All the better.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps I could give the figure now and save some time. I wish to finish up by six o'clock because if the committee will permit me I have some time to put in on another subject tonight in preparation for tomorrow evening.
How surprising.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The total to be reimbursed to the item of minor and unforeseen out of the present supplementary estimates now before the committee will be $828,100. The items where these reimbursements are to be found are Nos. 584, 595, 619, 620, 621, 643, 644, 647 and 655. The total of allotments and commitments in the present fiscal year to date was $1,556,623. Against that sum the $117,000 to which I have referred has been hitherto reimbursed leaving outstanding today $1,439,623 of allotments and commitments. With the reimbursement to which I have referred of $828,100 there will remain as a charge to the item provided in the main estimates a balance of $611,523.

If I may sum it up, the
minister thinks that for the remaining four months

or the three months and a bit-that remain of the fiscal year he is going to need over $2 million in a fund for which for the whole year he asked only $1.5 million?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is true. I wish to emphasize again the reasons that relate to the winter works program. We have brought it on as quickly as we can. The committee will appreciate that many of these programs just do not stop suddenly on March 31. In
