this area where we have been trying to accelerate the work creating programs as much as possible we find the reason for asking the committee to provide this additional sum to take care of the minor and unforeseen items.
Could I ask the minister one question? Does the minister not anticipate having any more supplementaries in the present fiscal year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There will be the usual final ones in March, those that are commonly known as the clean-up items.
B-Penitentiaries-
591. Construction, improvements, and equipment -further amount required, $315,000.

Mr. Chairman, may I call it six o'clock.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, I note from item 163 of the main estimates that the total amount asked for during the last session was $2,353,840. Of that amount, $900,000 roughly was for St. Vincent de Paul, Dorchester, Manitoba, British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Collin's Bay, federal training centre, Joyce-ville and so forth. In this supplementary item on the average a 24 per cent increase is asked for those institutions. Why are those amounts required?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Does my hon. friend ask me the question with respect to St. Vincent de Paul alone, or with respect to the whole item of $315,000?
All the institutions referred to, St. Vincent de Paul, Dorchester, British Columbia, Collin's Bay, federal training centre and Joyceville.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes; the 1961-62 estimates will contain, if approved by treasury board, certain construction proposals which it is considered are of sufficient urgency to justify asking authority to commence construction before the close of the present fiscal period. Those for which we are asking authority in these supplementary estimates to commence construction this winter include the following: at Dorchester penitentiary, an industrial building, $30,000, and an abattoir, $15,000; at St. Vincent de Paul, a penitentiary farm camp, $30,000; and a shops building, $40,000; at the federal training centre at St. Vincent de Paul, a vocational training building; $60,000; at Collin's Bay penitentiary.

Supply-Justice
an exercise hall, $60,000; at Joyceville, a shops building, $60,000; and at British Columbia, an exercise hall, $20,000.

How does the minister explain that as far as Dorchester is concerned in the estimates of 1958-59 the expenditures were $152,000 and in 1959-60 they were $150,000? In the 1960-61 main estimates they were $116,000 only, a reduction of $34,000. Those were the main estimates and an estimate of the expenditure should have been known at the time. At that time the Minister of Finance said we were going to have a surplus of $12 million. After reducing the estimates from $150,000 to $116,000 he comes back with a supplementary estimate and asks the committee for $45,000 more. This puts us in a strange position. The minister wanted to cut expenditures in order to get a surplus. He now comes back with a supplementary estimate which will make the total amount more than what was voted last year.
The same thing is true of the federal centre at St. Vincent de Paul. Does this amount apply only to Montreal or to all Canada? In 1958-59, $33,000 was voted; in 1959-60, $54,000 was voted; and in 1960-61, $147,000. The minister now asks for a further $60,000. I do not think the Minister of Justice can say that it was to give work to the unemployed because last summer and the summer before everybody knew there were people unemployed. Can the minister explain why it is that after reducing the amount spent in the previous year in order to produce a surplus he now comes back with a supplementary estimate which makes the amount larger than ever before?
Of course, he cannot tell the committee and the people of Canada that it is an unforeseen expense to provide employment for the people of Canada. Everybody knew there was unemployment last year and two years ago and also this year. What I do not understand is why the minister has waited so long to change the estimate of expenses in 1959 and 1960 in so far as the federal training centre is concerned. In 1960-61, $147,970 was voted for the federal training centre, and now the minister comes in with another supplementary estimate of $60,000. Surely, we are entitled to some kind of an explanation of these two points I have just mentioned. Dorchester, for instance, was reduced in 1960-61 by $34,000 as compared with 1959-60. Then, in the supplementary estimates the minister increases the amount by $45,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not know why my hon. friend should be so harsh with my very modest request for $315,000 in these supplementary estimates. If my hon. friend 
feels it is not necessary to improve the penitentiary system by this amount, that this is an unjustifiable estimate, I shall be very glad indeed to hear his points of criticism and try to meet them; but, as he knows, it is customary to present to parliament from time to time items in the supplementary estimates to cover projects which experience has shown can usefully be constructed to improve the operation of the whole program. It is in this spirit that we submit this item which I feel is well justified.

In almost every penitentiary there is a reduction and then an increase from the previous year. Take Collin's Bay, for instance. In 1958-59, $111,000 was voted; in 1959-60, $181,000 was voted. I do not know whether the Minister of Justice or the Minister of Finance wanted to show a decrease of expenditure in 1960-61. Then you come here today with another increase of $60,000. I should like to know what is going on. There was no unforeseen expenditure up until now. If the minister wants to explain that the additional $60,000 will give employment to some unemployed people, that will be fine with me provided he can prove it. Was the government not in a position to foresee these expenditures last June and July when the main estimates came before the house? I think the purpose of the government was that they wanted people to believe that now, after many deficits, we were going to have a surplus. They said to the people that unless there were unforeseen expenditures there would be a $12 million surplus this year. Right?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I never said anything of the sort.

That is what the Minister of Finance said and the Minister of Justice belongs to the same government. It was very nice for the government to tell the people of Canada that for once they were going to have a surplus. It was very easy to announce a surplus of $12 million when the government had in the back of their minds that through supplementary estimates they were going to make additional expenditures so that instead of having a surplus of $12 million it is possible that surplus will become a deficit of $12 million.
I do not see any unforeseen expenses as to the penitentiaries at Kingston, St. Vincent de Paul, Dorchester, Manitoba, British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Collin's Bay and the federal training centre. In almost every case there was a reduction in the main estimates so far as these penitentiaries are concerned and now the minister comes along with an increase. Is this an unforeseen expenditure or are more people going to be employed?

Is the purpose to employ more people and, if so, could the minister not have decided upon that during the month of July when the main estimates came before the house?

Mr. Chairman, I do not rise because I have any objection to the supplementary vote of $315,000 because I know that the money is required and I know that the house is going to have to ratify the expenditure of millions upon millions before our penal system is up to scratch. However,
I should like to ask the minister this question. Will the expenditure of the additional $315,000 give construction jobs to outside construction workers or is it going to be spent on the basis of the inmates doing the work so as to keep them out of mischief and so that they can learn a trade? Which is it going to be?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In answer to the last question I have to say that most of these items will represent contracts let to outside employers and the work will be done by outside labour. However, when I remind the hon. member of the nature of the project I think he will be able to see that they will make the useful employment and occupation of inmates in the institutions much more easy. It will give us the facilities for the useful occupation of inmates in the institutions.
At Dorchester, for instance, there is an industrial building which is designed to provide employment in three shops in manufacturing and finishing wood furniture and metal products. The shop design and the desire to get the project finished soon are of such a nature that it makes it appropriate to let the project to outside contract but when completed it will enable us to carry on a much better in-training program of the inmates of the institution.
With respect to the abattoir at Dorchester, I have to report that the present facilities for the slaughtering of cattle and hogs have been condemned by the department of health so we are not able to postpone the provision of better abattoir facilities.
Again, at St. Vincent de Paul we are asking for $30,000 to establish a penitentiary farm camp, that is, a camp on the penitentiary reserve itself. The construction of a farm camp will assist by providing living facilities for 80 inmates outside the walls of the main institution in healthy surroundings on the farm which forms part of the St. Vincent reserve. Then there is a shops building at St. Vincent de Paul which, when constructed, will enable us to provide employment in three shops, wood furniture manufacturing, tire reconditioning and centralized regional automotive repairs, which again will enable us to provide a better industrial training program at that penitentiary.
Supply-Justice
Another item is for the federal training centre-a vocational training building- which will contribute vitally toward the permanent rehabilitation of inmates who desire to learn a trade. This will provide shop accommodation and classroom facilities to train an additional 100 inmates at the federal training centre when it is completed.
So that with respect to this construction program I may say in general that although the construction itself is to be carried on by outside civilian contractors this will achieve three purposes. First, it will provide employment during the winter months. Second, it will give us better facilities, a considerable increase in the facilities with which we can provide in-training programs for inmates. Third, it will be an advance upon the construction program to which the hon. member for Vancouver East has referred, namely an over-all program of improving correctional institutions in Canada.
With respect to the strictures of the hon. member for St. Denis, again I find it is a little bit difficult to accept full responsibility for the diminution of the forecast surplus of $12 million simply because I submit this humble and modest item of $315,000 in the supplementary estimates for the penitentiaries branch. I think he is trying to heap on my shoulders a share of responsibility which is not quite appropriate to be landed there. However, I do remind him that I said at the beginning of my explanation that we have not represented this particular item so much as making up unforeseen expenditures during this fiscal year as we have put it forward as an advance on the construction program that would otherwise be entirely included in the main estimates of the next fiscal year.
All government departments have been asked to examine their potential construction programs and to bring forward any items that could profitably be started this winter for which their plans would otherwise have deferred until next year. We have accordingly brought forward from next year's plans these items for the penitentiaries branch which otherwise we would have deferred until next year.
That could have been done last spring.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We are bringing them forward now and, of course, in view of the very severe condemnation of this construction program by my hon. friend it is perhaps open to me to suggest that the reason why we do it now is that we might find him in a better spirit at this time of the year than we would have at any other time.

Supply-Justice

I do not say I am against the expenditures but expenditures of this kind could have been provided for last spring. They could have appeared in the main estimates and the work would have been already started now. You have decided on a winter program in the month of December. What is the use? When are they going to start? Have they started already?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, but I can assure the hon. member-

I do not want to use too harsh a word, but was the government asleep for two or three years? Did it just wake up? If the need for these expenditures could have been foreseen they could have been included in the main estimates.
I see the parliamentary secretary is laughing and smiling. I do not know if he is smiling or laughing at me or with me. However, I believe he will agree with me that this winter works program comes too late, as usual. I simply submit that these estimates should have been included in the main estimates in order to help the unemployed this winter. This money should not be voted in December but should have been voted earlier in the year, and that is what I want to know from the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If we are too late, then it is my responsibility and I ask my hon. friend to help me rectify the error by passing these supplementary estimates.

This vote is for $315,000. Can the minister advise how much of this money is for St. Vincent de Paul, how much for Dorchester, British Columbia, Collins Bay, the federal training centre and Joyceville? Can he tell us how much is for material and how much is for labour?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am not able to say exactly how much will be devoted to each of these subheadings because we have to wait until the item is approved before we can make the tender calls. It is only when we have made the tender calls that we will get a break-down of the contracts.
I had anticipated a question with regard to the number of jobs that this would create and I have done my best to find that out. I am advised, however, that until we have let the contracts I will not be able to give a definite figure. The projects contained in this item have been designed with two purposes in mind: First, to obtain an advance on our own construction program for next year and, second, by so doing to provide increased employment this winter. We are prepared to

defend each one of these projects as an essential part of the over-all penitentiary construction program. We are satisfied we can start this winter and thus be enabled to provide extra employment. However, I cannot, with the best will in the world, say exactly how many men will be employed on each job.
May I ask the minister how he is able to say these projects will cost only $315,000 if the plans are not prepared and the specifications have not been prepared?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I can say that very readily because that is the limit of the authority we will have. We cannot spend more than $315,000 at this time because parliament will not have authorized more than that. You must remember also, Mr. Chairman, that in several cases this money will be advanced on construction projects, the continuation of which will be authorized in the main estimates for 1961-02. These will not necessarily be the limits of the projects themselves, and a whole project may well, in some cases, cost more than this. This is another reason why I cannot say at the moment how much will go for materials and how much for labour. We will be discussing with the contractors who tender the possibility of arranging their work during these winter months so as to provide the maximum of jobs during that season.
This is just giving a blank cheque. You have no definite projects?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is no blank cheque; No, we are asking for authority to spend $315,000 between now and March 31, and no more than that. We would have no authority to spend any more. All I am saying is that some of these projects may not be completed by March 31, in which case we would have to include a further item in the main estimates and come back to parliament to ask for more money.
Is there going to be a proviso in the contracts under which the unemployed will get priority in so far as the labourers are concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman, in accordance with the policy of the government administered through the Department of Labour's winter works program. May I give an example to my hon. friend for Levis? The first project included in this item, Dorchester penitentiary industrial building, is estimated to cost $161,000. It is estimated we can usefully spend $30,000 during the period up to March 31, 1961.
I should like to know from the minister how many man hours are going to be spent by the inmates and how many by outsiders?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This program, Mr. Chairman, does not envisage the employment of inmate labour on construction. These projects will all be built by outside contractors.
Are the contracts let now or are they going to be let?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I believe some tenders have been called in anticipation, but so far as I am aware none of the contracts have been signed as yet. Treasury board approval would be required before that could be done.
May I ask if the plans have been prepared by the departmental architects or by outside architects?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: These plans have all been prepared by the engineering and architectural division of the penitentiaries branch.

I notice in the main estimates under this heading the amount for St. Vincent de Paul is $157,675; for Dorchester, $116,135; for British Columbia, $97,770; for Collins Bay, $164,280; for the federal training centre, $147,970 and for Joyceville, $216,425. The total amount requested in the supplementary estimates is $315,000. The break-down of this item is as follows: St. Vincent de Paul, $70,000; Dorchester, $45,000; British Columbia, $20,000; Collins Bay, $60,000; federal training centre, $60,000 and Joyceville, $60,000. This makes an aggregate increase of 34 per cent. When the main estimates were prepared was it possible to foresee that the work to be done on these institutions would add up to $1,250,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
At any one time any department of government could spend far more money, if it were left on its own, than treasury board includes in the estimates. I have explained earlier in connection with this item, however, that this is not so much supplementary estimates to make up some deficiency in the current year's authorized expenditures as it is an advance on next year's construction program. We had a construction program for this year and we have a construction program for next year as well as one for the year after. What all departments, including my own, were asked to do in connection with this year's winter works program was to re-examine their construction program to see how much they could bring forward for this winter which otherwise would not have been done until next year. We so assessed our next year's building program and have brought this portion of it forward because we have been advised that this amount of work could profitably be started and carried out during the winter months of this year.
Supply-J ustice

Then you are saying that in March or April of last year this government did not know there was going to be a lack of employment this winter, and the government decided to increase employment by asking the committee to pass these further estimates?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This item is before the committee now in the same way that a number of other items are before the committee as projects designed to create employment during the winter months. I can only submit them in that spirit and ask the committee to approve them on that account. If the committee desires not to approve them, we shall be obliged to defer them until next year.
Let us suppose that there was no session at this time. Those people who are going to get employment would be obliged to wait until February. Would that be an emergency session or a regular session?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I could make a great many explanations on the basis of hypothetical assumptions but I am dealing with my supplementary estimates on the basis of the session having started on November 17. The session did start on November 17. I am here before the committee with this estimate on the basis of which, if approved, useful employment will be provided and a useful advance will be provided on the penitentiary construction program.
Am I right in understanding that this amount of $315,000 is for new works that are going to be constructed until March 31? Are these new works?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. We have no money in the 1960-61 estimates for the purpose. We would otherwise have had to wait until the 1961-62 main estimates. In general we have brought forward this amount for a start on the increased construction program. On looking at my notes I find that this is not completely accurate with respect to the vocational training building at St. Vincent de Paul federal training centre. I find there that $30,000 has already been voted for this project this year and we are asking for an additional $60,000 this year because we think we can finish it before March 31, the total cost being $90,000.

How is it that the whole amount was not voted in the main estimates? Plans must have been made. Estimates must have been calculated. I do not see why the minister is coming along at this time and asking us for an additional amount of $50,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am coming back now because we did not get the $60,000 in our main estimates. That is why I am back here. If I had

Supply-Justice
the $60,000, I can assure my hon. friend I would not be here before the committee.
Then it was refused by the treasury board, was it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It was not included in the main estimates.
For what reason? For the reason that it was refused by the treasury board. That is the reason.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It certainly was not included by the treasury board.
The minister can say what he likes; it was refused.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If my hon. friend is labouring to produce a gnat and says that the treasury board did not authorize the amount in the main estimates, he is quite right. He knows how treasury board works.
I do not know. I was not a minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have had the same answer on many occasions. I have said, and I will say it again, that we are asking for this money because it was not included in the main estimates this year and we can usefully do this work in the winter months. If the committee thinks we should do it, I hope they will approve this vote.
The answer is obvious. The question we are asking is why it was not possible, when the main estimates were brought down, to embody these amounts that are now being asked for.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Again, as my hon. friends know very well,-
I do not know. I was not here.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am sorry but I did not catch what my hon. friend said.
I said I did not know; I was not here in the previous year.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: But my hon. friend was here when the main estimates were being voted for this year?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
All the explanations necessary to support the items in the main estimates were given at that time. It is well known to all the members of the committee that when you are estimating what it will be possible to spend in one year and are then dividing up year construction program between 1960-61 and 1961-62, an error of $60,000 in a vote of say nearly $1 million for individual construction items is not untoward. The government has asked all the departments to reassess their reconstruction programs. As I recall it,

the members of the opposition strongly urged that the government should reassess its construction program. We have complied with both these requests and are bringing forward an item for $315,000 which I can assure my hon. friends can be properly and usefully spent on this construction program this winter. Unless my hon. friends think that we should not provide this employment, I would hope they might allow this item to pass.

It is about time the minister gave the real reason, namely that they made an error at that time. Do not tell the people that you are asking for $60,000 in order to help employment but rather that you made an error of $60,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There was no error made unless it was that of assuming that my friend the hon. member for St. Denis understood the explanation we gave on the earlier occasion.
What was the estimated cost of the federal training centre for which the amount is listed here as $60,000 in the supplementary estimates?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This is on the vocational training building at the federal training centre. In the 1960-61 estimates $30,000 was included for initial construction on this project. We now estimate that we can advance construction to the extent of a further $60,000 by March 31. This is not to say that this is the total amount that will be required for construction of this building.
Did I understand the minister to say that $30,000 was included in the main estimates?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

Surely the minister will agree with me that any company or any contractor can spend more than $30,000. We have the $60,000 asked for in the supplementary estimates and the $30,000 voted in the main estimates. Surely this amount could have been expended during the fiscal year 1960-61. Either there was a lack of design or a lack of provision. There is no other answer that could be given. Surely any contractor can do some work for $90,000 in a fiscal year.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Oh, yes, indeed; and of course it would be possible to accelerate all of your construction programs and thereby increase the cost of construction, as was done on some occasions by the government in which my hon. friend was a parliamentary assistant, as he should remember. But the question is the extent to which you should accelerate your construction program and therefore increase the cost of construction. It was therefore, I submit, a perfectly proper thing for this government to do when it included in the

main estimates the amounts which it thought could be properly expended in accordance with the normal construction program and then, at a time when it became desirable, to revise its construction program in the light of winter unemployment and then to decide to what extent it should accelerate that construction program by bringing forward parts of it which would otherwise be deferred until the next year: That is exactly what we have done. The $60,000 with respect to this particular project represents an accelerated pace of construction of this vocational training building.

Surely the minister will agree with me that when we passed the main estimates, under which $30,000 was voted, that was the time at which to vote more. When the estimates were passed we knew there was a great deal of unemployment and at the time we could foresee a great deal more unemployment occurring this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If I had included in the main estimates the whole amount which is now under discussion my hon. friends would have accused me of accelerating construction programs and wasting the people's money.

No, we never said that. As a matter of fact, we will be voting $30 million in a few minutes for winter employment. On the other hand, when you take the construction items of all the departments which take care of construction we have deducted $73 million out of that program of construction.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Is my hon. friend prepared to pass items in the supplementary estimates for the purpose of providing winter employment, or is he not?
I am.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Then I do not know why my hon. friend is holding up this very modest, humble item of $315,000 in respect of the whole-
Because you have given a very bad explanation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
-penitentiary construction
program in Canada as though this single grant to one department were responsible for all the ills which my hon. friends say they foresee for this country of ours.

The only reason I rose is because, as I said, the government had no plans at all until faced today with the situation of having more than 400,000 unemployed. That is the reason they are now bringing some items forward to increase construction. That is the reason I rose, because I want to repeat that the government has no plans at all to
Supply-J ustice
face up to the situation which the Canadian people are now facing with over 400,000 unemployed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I assure my hon. friend that I have extensive plans for a penitentiaries construction program.
That is the time to do it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If my hon. friend would restrain his enthusiasm for a moment and think of this calmly, and then if in accordance with what I would regard as a constructive approach he would, when my main estimates are before the committee-as they were last spring and will be again this coming year- urge that there should be more money devoted to the penitentiaries construction program, I shall be glad indeed to receive his support.
It seems to me that that is the time to express this support, instead of now, when I bring forward this modest item to make a contribution to help solve the present unemployment problem in Canada, raising petty points and quibbling because there was not this modest amount raised last year, which we have now included in the supplementary program.

I do not know if the Minister of Justice was in the house when I was speaking for the opposition on the public works estimates. At that time I mentioned the fact-and he can refer to my speech-that just on the Department of Public Works estimates there was a deduction of $25 million in the construction item. I would also like to add that we have never opposed any construction item. Far from it; we have asked the government to do more, and we blamed the government for deducting $25 million just on the public works program.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am asking for only $315,000. I hope my hon. friend will support it.
You will get it.
May I ask the minister the number of inmates who are in penitentiaries, compared to last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The number of inmates is just over 6,200.
I wonder if the minister would say if I am correct in interpreting what he said, that included in this estimate is money for the commencement of projects the ultimate costs of which are unknown.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, I have not the total costs for these projects. I do not have all the figures before me at the moment because that is a matter I expect to present during my main estimates.

Supply-Labour

Does the minister think it is appropriate to tell the committee what the ultimate costs will be, without giving details? It is something like giving a woman a cheque to buy a hat, when ultimately you know you will have to pay for a dress, a hat and other accessories.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is a matter about which my hon. friend knows more than I, being in that business. However, in my main estimates I expect to give the total costs of all these projects. I can give some now. The shops building at St. Vincent de Paul is estimated to cost a total of $110,000, of which we are asking for $40,000 at this time. The farm camp at the St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary is estimated to cost a total of $225,000, of which we are asking for an advance of $30,000 at this time. The shops building at Joyceville is estimated to cost a total of $150,000, of which we are asking for an advance of $60,000 at this time. The exercise hall, British Columbia, is estimated to cost a total of $50,000, of which we are asking for an advance of $20,000 at this time.
And in only one case is the construction already underway with the previous expenditure which has been authorized by parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, I think that is correct.
Item agreed to.
Normally the R.C.M.P. item comes under the estimates of the Minister of Justice. I think the committee would be agreeable to going to item 642 right away.

Marine services-
642. Construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and equipment-further amount required, $25,000.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it the wish of the committee to go to item 642 right away?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall item 642 carry?

Item agreed to.
DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR Special services-
592. Payments, in accordance with terms and conditions approved by the governor in council, to provinces and in respect of Indian bands under the municipal winter works incentive program during the 1960-61 and 1961-62 fiscal years of amounts not exceeding one half of the cost of labour incurred in the period from the loth day of October, 1960, to such day in the fiscal year 1961-62 as may be determined by the governor in council, $30,000,000.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, is the minister going to make a statement?

I did not get a chance. Thank you very much. I am happy to report that the principal item of some $30 million in these estimates relates to the municipal winter works program.
You will recall that last year the amount was $15 million. This has now been doubled and I may say that the program in this expanded form has met with a tremendous response across Canada. You will recall that the municipal winter works program arose from the unemployment conference which was held in July, 1958. In that first winter work was provided for some 35,000 men on site. Last year the number was in the neighbourhood of 50,000 on site.
I should explain that these figures refer, as I mentioned, to on-site employment; but I would like to make it quite clear that for every person employed on site there is at least one other person employed or given employment off site in the provision of materials and equipment. The estimate which I have received for this winter is that some 100,000 men will be given employment on site and an equal number will be kept in employment off site as a result of this program.
I have said that the program is being well received. An indication of this is that the latest figures in my possession as of December 16 reveal that on that date some 4,589 projects had been accepted from the municipalities across Canada. I may say that this program has provided very important assistance to the municipalities in this country.
Can you give us the provinces, the areas?
If the hon. member would be good enough to withhold that question we will be able to give him that information.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: You gave it last year.
I beg your pardon?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: You gave this earlier. When we discussed the main estimates at the former session you gave a break-down of this for the date up to the time of the discussion. We are hopeful that you will be able to do the same thing now.

Yes. I am just making a general statement on this item, and I will endeavour to supply all the information that will be required by the committee.
I may say that this program has provided very important assistance to the municipalities in this country. In the first place it has provided an easement in the financial position of a number of municipalities in relation to the undertaking of needed public works. It has made possible the undertaking of these works. It has brought forward a

large number of projects which otherwise would not have been undertaken and it has, of course, provided needed employment. I want to emphasize that this measure is one of a series of measures designed to maintain economic stability and to provide employment. When taken together these measures form the most comprehensive program of this kind ever placed before the parliament of Canada. In my opinion-and it is not just a matter of opinion because the figures are there-the municipal winter works program has been constructive, positive and effective.
I want to say that the results of the program to date this year are compiled in eight black bound books which hon. members see before them showing exactly what has been happening in every city, town and province under this program. As I mentioned earlier, I am happy to place this information at the disposal of any hon. member who wishes to question me on it.
As this program has gone on it has attained wider and wider acceptance. For example, the number of applications received to date is already almost over 2,000 more than that of last year's program. I may say that already at this date projects calling for a total expenditure of some $203 million have been approved. This will provide work for more than 78,000 men. To put it another way, the number of man days worked comes to 3,579,320 already. As the committee knows, the program came into effect this year on October 15, six weeks earlier than in previous years. I hope that this change will meet the approval of those who suggested last year that the program in addition to being too little was also too late. I think they will agree that this year it is neither. It is doubled in scope. It is six weeks earlier in time. In addition to that, it is considerably enlarged in substance.
This year, for example, we have added municipal buildings. This change has been welcomed with enthusiasm by the municipalities. We have also expanded the program by the addition of street lighting, traffic signals and municipal parking lots. We have also added pumping stations, filtration plants and sewage disposal plants. Meanwhile we have retained the projects of the past two years such as the construction and improvements of streets, roads, sidewalks and bridges, water, sewage and drainage facilities as well as parks and playgrounds. All in all the present program-the program embodied in this estimate-is the most extensive construction ever undertaken in the field of federal, provincial and municipal co-operation.
One of the happy features of the program is that it permits joint action and joint costsharing so that no one government is required to bear the whole burden. The administration
Supply-Labour
is carried on at the provincial level and the resulting provincial co-operation has been most gratifying. The federal government, as the committee knows, pays 50 per cent of the payroll costs of these projects. Five provinces are contributing an additional 25 per cent. One province is contributing 40 per cent. One province pays 25 per cent of direct payroll costs in respect of persons not entitled to unemployment insurance benefits and an additional 25 per cent in respect of persons in receipt of social allowances.
What province pays 40 per cent?
Quebec. That in general terms is the program that this estimate represents.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I believe the committee will be interested in the information which the minister has given to us. We will, of course, require a great deal more information as the discussion proceeds. I believe that all of us will want to assist the minister in getting an item of this importance through the committee promptly in the hope that it will be of some assistance to those who are unemployed during the course of the present winter.
I cannot say the same thing about the other programs to which the minister referred in general terms and of course I refer now to the legislation passed within the last few weeks, the amendments to the housing act, the small business legislation, the vocational training legislation and the legislation establishing the productivity council. As the minister knows, there is little if any at all of that legislation which will be of any use during the course of the present winter.
Good as this program is and good as it appears on the face of it, as the minister himself has admitted, in the first year of its operation the winter works program provided work for 35,000 people in this country. In 1959 it provided work for 50,000 people. The minister estimates that during the present year-although he is not able to give us firm figures-there will be provided on-site employment for about 100,000. When one considers that the unemployed figure for the middle of November amounted to well over 400,000, namely 428,000-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
-429,000, and when at the time at which I am speaking there has perhaps been a substantial increase, the committee can get some idea of just where this program fits in the over-all picture. It is a program that is directed at winter works and seasonal employment, and it is also one largely directed toward the construction industry. There are, of course, other parts of

Supply-Labour
the economy that are suffering because of unemployment and they are not in the construction industry.
One of the questions which now comes to my mind is this. Has the minister given any consideration to the representations which were made to him during the course of the dominion-provincial conference in October of this year? I refer now particularly to the representations made by the premier of the province of Quebec. The minister will probably remember the brief which was read by the premier at the time. Perhaps the hon. gentleman will allow me to put on the record just one paragraph from the brief and then ask him what consideration, if any, has been given to this aspect of the winter works program as suggested by the premier of Quebec. I quote from his statement:
(Translation):
The tact remains, however, that a well thought-out works program could be helpful, particularly in wintertime, in stimulating the construction industry and related industries. In that connection, I should like to make a practical suggestion which I think would add greatly to the beneficial effects of the joint winter works program. At the present time, contributions paid to the municipalities are standardized and cover only part of the labour costs. The main cost of such works therefore remains a municipal responsibility.
Such a situation is not too hard on the more prosperous municipalities where there is little unemployment. Federal and provincial subsidies enable them to reduce their financial burden. However, the present system of standard contributions does not allow the poorer municipalities to fully share in the winter works program, despite the fact that, as a general rule, they have a higher proportion of unemployed. Under the direct control of the provinces, there might be established a system of subsidies scaled according to the proportion of unemployed.
(Text):
This is the part to which I have particular reference:
(Translation):
In such a case, maximum contributions should cover part of the cost of machinery and equipment. We hope this suggestion will be discussed in further detail during this conference.
(Text):
Among the suggestions made by the premier of Quebec were these two. One had to do with a distinction which might well be made between the poorer municipalities- if I may use that expression-as compared with the wealthier ones and the other was the question of the federal government paying a part of the cost of the machinery and equipment. The suggestion has been made by the hon. member for Levis that I should enquire what consideration, if any, has been given to paying a portion of the cost of the materials as well as the cost of the machinery and equipment as suggested by the premier.

When the minister has an opportunity will he give consideration to this aspect of the case?
My main purpose in rising, was to discuss another aspect of this problem and one where I think the federal government has completely fallen down. I have reference now to the distress areas in Canada. What is the policy of the federal government with reference to those areas? There are in Canada at the present time many distress areas; certainly, I do not want to give them any publicity by mentioning them, but I do hold in my hand a number of publications, one of which is the Labour Gazette of May 20, and another is the same publication of January 21, 1960. In this publication a definition is given of the classes in which various communities are placed in Canada. Some are placed in group one, where there is a labour surplus and which are defined as areas in which current or immediately prospective labour supply exceeds demand in almost all of the major occupations. Then, there is the group two labour surplus area in which current or immediately prospective labour supply exceeds demand in about half of the major occupations. There is a third group where there is a balanced labour supply, and a fourth group where there is a labour shortage.
I propose to deal with the first two only and then as it affects the policy of the government. What is the policy of the government with respect to those areas where there is a labour surplus? The Labour Gazette to which I referred earlier deals with a number of those areas in our country. It has occurred to me that in one of those at least, not to mention the others, there is a serious situation. The only reason I mention it is that in the last few weeks considerable attention has been paid to it on television and elsewhere. I refer to the city of Cornwall where, as the committee and the minister knows particularly, there is a very serious labour surplus. I am wondering what, if anything, the federal government has done to meet the stiuation in that area? I do know that at the present time there is an application by the Hydro Electric Power Commission of Ontario before the national energy board for permission of that corporation to export power to the United States when that commission refuses to grant power to two local power companies which could assist the community.
I call upon the national energy board to give careful consideration to that application and to make sure that that application on the part of the Hydro Electric Power Commission to export power outside Canada is not granted when there is a demand for it in eastern Ontario, and particularly when that commission

in the province of Ontario refuses to set aside a block of power for industry in eastern Ontario, whereas on the opposite side of the boundary line in the state of New York power has been set aside for industry. I call upon the minister to tell the committee what is the policy of the government with reference to to those distressed areas.
I should like to put on Hansard a summary of what is being done in other countries, if I may. There is a policy in Great Britain having to do with distress areas. It has existed throughout the years since 1934. Incentives there exist to induce companies to settle in distressed areas and they have gradually been made more generous. Since 1946, these incentives have consisted of factory construction for rental purposes; grants loaned to companies wishing to build their own factories, and the improvement of basic services, such as road, utilities and the like. Of course, I understand that in our country, because of our constitution, the latter suggestion would not come under the jurisdiction of the federal government.
Under the law in May, 1960 the board of trade has power (1) to acquire land by agreement and build factories for lease; (2) to give building grants amounting to 85 per cent of the difference between the actual cost of the construction of a private plant and the value of the building on completion; (3) to extend substantial loans or grants to private enterprise; and (4) to acquire land which is abandoned or neglected and improve it so that it may be brought into use or may improve property values in the neighbourhood.
In Belgium there is a program having to do with surplus labour in certain areas of that country. Aid to labour surplus areas in Belgium is still in the first stages of development, although the desirability of providing national assistance to certain regions has been much talked of since 1945. No major measures were undertaken toward this end until the enactment of what is known as the regional development law of July 18, 1959. This legislation recognizes the need to attract industry to areas which have labour surpluses. Incentives for this purpose are provided in the form of loans, grants, tax exemptions and government construction of factories for lease.
In Germany, where there was a very substantial labour surplus area in 1951, as a result of the program which was established and put into operation there, as the committee knows, the contrary exists today and there is a labour shortage. A wide variety of assistance is available in that country depending on the requirements of a specific
Supply-Labour
area. In 1959, assistance measures included the following:
(1)	loans for industrial and handicraft enterprises;
(2)	loans and interest subsidies for tourist enterprises;
(3)	loans and grants to public or private non-profit organizations established to improve the general economic conditions in an area;
(4)	loans and grants for agriculture improvement, vocational training and for the improvement of public facilities, such as roads, electricity and water.
In Sweden, in contrast to the three countries I have mentioned, there is no program to aid specifically designated labour surplus areas. Instead the Swedish program is designed to go into effect in any area at any time. It is, if you like, legislation in abeyance, ready to be applied to any ad hoc situation. Measures for aiding labour surplus areas consist of (1) assisting the unemployed to move; (2) promoting the location of new business in an area: (3) public works.
Therefore, from the discusion or the mention of what is happening in those four countries one fact emerges. It is that all of them have recognized the existence of the problem. They have all designated certain areas as being labour surplus areas. They have established programs to aid these areas. They have made progress in assisting these areas to improve their employment opportunities.
The question that naturally arises is, what have we done in Canada in this regard? Do we have legislation specifically designed to meet the needs of labour surplus areas? Have we studied the experience of the European countries in this regard? It is true that in dealing with the matter now before the committee the minister mentioned a while ago that the program was a most comprehensive one, but the fact is that the program, as the house knows, is directed toward one aspect of the economy only and is not directed toward the whole of the economy. It deals with one basic industry, namely construction, and does not deal with the others. Neither does this nor any other part of the program deal with structural unemployment or unemployment arising out of automation. Certainly there is, as far as I can see, no determination to meet the problem in distressed areas.
I wonder what the government has in mind with reference to such areas because while I mentioned one I have four others in my mind at the moment which I do not want to mention lest unfavourable publicity be given to them and lest I be accused by those who sit on the other side of the house of casting gloom and perhaps also of doing a disservice

Supply-Labour
to these communities. I hope that before this item goes through the minister will be in a position to tell the house just what the plans are for dealing with these areas, one of which I have mentioned, because I know that their plight is serious.

Mr. Chairman, I have had an interesting time listening to the hon. member for Laurier advocating this new found form of creeping socialism, something which he abhorred and rejected not too long ago when he sat on the other side of the house. I must say that it certainly sounded convincing. It sounded fine and I am sure it will read nicely in Hansard. However, there are a number of members in the house who know better and realize that this latter-day reformation of the Liberals that the hon. member for Laurier is trying to promote has a few drawbacks and perhaps will not get too far, even if he meant that this should become a part of Liberal philosophy.
He talked about economic planning but in reality we know that all he and the Liberal party are talking about is economic plotting, or perhaps one should say political plotting, in the hope that this will raise the standard of that party in the eyes of the general public some time in the future when we may have a test of strength in the country. My friend behind me says that it is quite high now. I remember that there was an election in British Columbia not too long ago and it is the only place in the whole country where Liberal party support dropped percentage-wise and also in total vote, so it is not too good there.
But this is one of the gratifying things that comes about by reason of the Liberals having been forced out of office for becoming stagnant and from the development of the new party, a new political force in Canada which is making some people think and wonder what sort of projects they should push in order to promote employment and take care of our economy. The situation has probably pushed the Liberals into a quandary because I do not see how even they can justify this stand on the one hand and attempt to reform Joey Smallwood on the other, he representing the rightist element of that party. As I say. the hon. member's remarks sounded fine and they will probably read well but the general public will remember the 22 long years that the Liberals were in power and people will perhaps not be quite so trusting as the Liberal party hopes they will be.
These remarks, of course, do not get at the basis of the particular item now before us. Needless to say, the pronouncements of the hon. member for Laurier about economic planning and dealing with distressed areas
[Mr. Chevrier.j
represent the expression of an admirable point of view. I doubt very much whether the Liberals really believe it or whether the Tory government will put it into effect but it is something that has been sadly needed for a long, long time, something that has been advocated by the socialist element in Canada for many years and which has been rejected by these arch free enterprisers. In fact, I am quite sure that if such an economic system of planning for distressed areas had been promoted when the hon. member for Laurier was the member for Stormont, Cornwall would not be in so much difficulty as it is today provided there had been something on the statute books to deal with the situation.
This so-called winter works incentive program appears to be the major and key part of the Conservative government's campaign to deal with the economy and to promote employment. Certainly the measures we have dealt with up to now during this session have had relatively little in them that would deal with the question immediately. Because they have touted this program for quite a number of years now and placed a good deal of emphasis on it, it would appear to be the major and key part of the government's campaign to deal with the economy and to attempt to get people back to work. There is no question that it will be of some help. With respect to certain projects of which I am aware it has already assisted in putting people to work so that they can accomplish something useful rather than remaining idle and collecting rocking chair money or not collecting anything at all.
It is helpful that the minister listened to what he was told when the plan was first instituted and what those on this side of the house said during the last session and as a result has undertaken to expand the type of work which can be engaged in under this plan. The unfortunate part is that this program, like so many others instituted by people with the political philosophy of those in the Tory party, was forced upon the government rather than being the result of leadership or imagination.
Hear, hear.

The economic conditions of the nation are what promote this sort of action. The hon. member for Essex East says "hear, hear". I am sure if he reflects he will recall that I referred to governments that have this particular political philosophy.
We have been pushing this matter for three years.

My friend has been advocating almost anything for the last three years as long as it would tend to improve the position

of his party. I am advocating, as I always have, those things which I think are sensible and right and by which I hope to place myself and the party to which I belong in a more acceptable position than we are. The only thing is that I admit it, unlike my friends who spent 22 years in arrogance and double talk, still want to engage in the same sort of thing and refuse to admit these facts of political life.
It was the collapse or near collapse of our economy a few years ago that really forced the government into some sort of patchwork program, and that is all this winter works incentive program is, another patch on the leaky, old free enterprise boat. It will help a little bit, but it will not solve the over-all problem. It is something that is acceptable because it will be helpful in that regard.
However, when we consider the fact that municipalities are going to get some assistance for certain types of jobs, and when we consider the exorbitant high interest rates they have to pay on the money they borrow, interest rates forced upon them by this government's foolish fiscal policies, then we wonder whether the help will be worth while. There are municipalities in my own constituency that have balanced these two things and have come to the conclusion they will not be any better off in terms of dollars. They have come to the conclusion they will be in debt and their interest rates will be higher over the long haul, so they will not be any better off under this particular program.
I think it would have been more advisable if the government, or the Liberals before them, had embarked upon a municipal lending fund, a revolving fund for the municipalities from which they could borrow at low interest rates to assist them in the development of municipal services. I am sure if something of that nature had been done a long time ago it would have prevented the municipalities from being driven around the bend as a result of their activities in Wall street. Perhaps our municipalities would now be in a much better position than they are today.
I feel that there are some weaknesses in the program that is advocated here, and I have communicated with the minister about one of them. I refer to the extension of this program to what is known as unorganized territories, that is areas which are not organized into municipalities, cities, towns or municipal districts. We have a number of them in British Columbia. I wrote the minister about one such area in which the people, because of the rural electrification program of the British Columbia power commission, wanted to extend the rural electrification into
Supply-Labour
Burns Lake. This is not an organized district but the people of the area are in a position, because of British Columbia's hydro policy, to provide some of the work and some of the material themselves. They wanted to participate in this federal program in order to clear the right of way for the power line, for digging the holes for poles, for providing the poles, cutting them and skidding them. They wanted to engage in some sort of participation financially with this government in that sort of project. I think it is an admirable type of project, and if we are going to have this sort of program we should extend it to jobs of this type.
In British Columbia-I do not know whether the same thing applies in other provinces-we have local improvement districts organized from time to time. They are not municipalities but are sort of ad hoc groupings of people who want to establish a water system or a sewage system, something of that nature. They establish a local improvement district and can actually borrow money with the backing of the provincial government. I believe this type of community should be included in this program. I do not see why because one person happens to live in a city and another person lives in a rural area, the person in the rural area should be placed at a disadvantage when it comes to assistance in providing local services such as the cities provide.
Apart from this and some discussion of specific details, I doubt very much whether one can contribute any more at this time. I would say that for many, many years we have wholeheartedly endorsed the idea of government assistance to industries in geographic areas and communities in which those industries are most needed. If necessary government financial assistance should be provided to ensure that industries are established in those areas in which they are needed most. The result of the lax sort of program we have at the moment is that industries will build where the services are available or where raw materials are available because this is their prime concern. They are not concerned that an industry be established where a number of people happen to live, and I think this should be the prime concern. We have seen a number of instances of so-called runaway plants which have resulted from this lax policy. Industries will be bought out by some large company, the facilities closed down and moved to another part of the country. This happened in Nova Scotia on a number of occasions and plants were closed down and moved into Ontario where there were more services. This is a serious hardship to the communities involved and the working people themselves.

Supply-Labour
This is one of the aspects in which the government should become engaged. We hope they do not become engaged in it merely because of the force of economic pressures. We would rather that the government become engaged in this sort of assistance program to the communities, the so-called distressed areas, and become involved from the humanitarian point of view of what will be beneficial to the people themselves rather than, as I said earlier, be pushed into it by the force of economic pressures.

I wonder if the minister could give us some break-down of some of the generalizations he has given. He has told us, for instance, that there are 4,989 projects as of December 16. Could he tell us how these are broken down as between the various provinces?

The break-down is, British Columbia, 489; Alberta, 538; Saskatchewan, 554; Manitoba, 191; Ontario, 1,137; Quebec, 1,287; New Brunswick, 145; Nova Scotia, 91; Prince Edward Island, 13; Newfoundland, 104; Yukon, 1; Indian bands, 39.
Could we have a break-down as between the cities in Ontario? For instance, how many are there in Cornwall?
In Cornwall, there are seven projects under way.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: For how much?

The number of men employed, 173; man days worked, 11,229; cost of the projects, $358,339; the payroll costs, $117,251; government share, $58,401. I must give you the pay in the period from October 15 to the end of April, and that is estimated at $117,251, which gives the government's share of $58,401.
Can the minister tell me how many projects there are in Peterborough?
There are 22 projects in Peterborough: number of men involved, 368; man days work, 11,293; total cost, $1,154,452; payroll cost for the period, $155,341; government share, $77,676.

I asked for some of these particulars Mr. Chairman, because they reveal the essential weakness of this program. No one denies the fact that any program that will put some people to work at this time is a desirable one. We have always taken the position in this party during the past three years, that this program would be supported by us, not because we regard it as an answer to the problem but because it was capable of putting a limited number of people to work. However, on the basis

of the figures the minister has given showing the number of projects in our ten provinces and the number of men thus far who have been put to work in certain communities, where unemployment is extremely high, it is surely evident how limited this program in fact is.
The hon. member who last spoke, the hon. member for Skeena, in noting with satisfaction the review made by the hon. member for Laurier, sought to indicate that his statement represented a change of attitude on our part. The hon. member, of course, forgets that during the past three years in this chamber it has been left to the Liberal members of parliament to prod the government, to urge the government to do something, in the matter of unemployment. It has been left to the members of the Liberal party each session- and the record is there for everyone to see- to urge the government to announce its policy with regard to the ensuing winter works program. Then when that policy was announced, it was again mainly left to the same party members in this chamber to criticize the measure. Hence when the hon. member for Skeena takes unto himself the responsibility for saying that the suggestions made by the hon. member for Laurier represent a change of attitude, and one prompted by political considerations, he is not addressing himself to the proposal in proper context, as I am sure he himself realizes.
We in this party take second place to no group in this House of Commons with regard to what we have sought to do during the past three years to bring home to the government its responsibility in this matter and its failure adequately to cope with the problem. As a matter of fact, if the hon. member for Skeena will go back and look up Hansard he will find that early last session the hon. member for Laurier, in listing 25 different proposals of the Liberal party in the matter of unemployment, listed as No. 8 the suggestion that the government should concentrate its attention on surplus labour areas, to assess the economic factors at work in them and1 to establish the means of providing work in those areas. Hence to suggest that in advocating that the government should make an attack on the distressed areas-
A concentration.

-or a concentration on the distressed areas, we are advocating tonight anything different from what we have been advocating for some time now in this chamber is erroneous.
Let us consider, for example, the figures the minister has given for Cornwall and for Peterborough. I believe that the unemployment figures in those two communities represent, in terms of the percentage of the

labour force that is out of work, perhaps as high a figure as will be found in almost any city of our country. In Cornwall where the population is about 40,000, some 4,000 or 5,000 people are out of work. Those are the statistics. I may be out a couple of hundred; perhaps it is 4,000 but it is in that neighbourhood. I was in Cornwall about seven weeks ago. I paid some attention to the problem of unemployment in that city. I am now speaking from memory, but my recollection is that in that community there were between 4,000 and 4,500 unemployed out of a population, as I said, of 40,000 people. The minister has told us that this particular program has resulted in seven projects being accepted by the province and by the municipality for Cornwall and that it has put to work some 173 people.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: No, no.

That is what the minister said. The minister gave those figures. Then he came to Peterborough. He said that in Peterborough there were 22 projects and that as a result it was estimated that work would be provided for some 368 people. Those are the figures given by the minister. I do not have before me the exact number of unemployed in Peterborough. However, I should think that I am not wrong-and the hon. member for Peterborough who is not in his seat at the moment, and I am not criticizing him for that fact, could possibly give confirmation-when I say that the unemployment figure in Peterborough is in the neighbourhood of 4,000 to 5,000.
Does anyone seriously suggest that in this period of emergency a program that can put to work in Peterborough only 368 men and in Cornwall only 173 men represents a real, dynamic, well thought out program designed to take care of unemployment?
I could talk about my own city in which there are nearly 11,000 people out of work. Can the minister tell me how many projects have been accepted for Windsor and how many men have been put to work or are estimated will be put to work?
There are 13 projects; 219 men.

The minister says there are 13 projects and that 219 men will be put to work, it is estimated. In a community with almost 11,000 unemployed, 219 men are given work by this program, the major effort of the federal government to deal with this problem of unemployment. Do we need to go any further than merely recite these figures to establish the inadequacy of this program? As I said, to the extent that this program will give work at all, it must be supported. But because this program now has been able to encourage the existence of
Supply-Labour
4,989 projects in the country the government must not think that it is on that account able to discharge its responsibility to the people of Canada with respect to this problem.
Undoubtedly the government is pursuing the development of this program in the following manner: it is saying to the provinces, "We are prepared to pay 50 per cent of the cost of projects in respect of wages paid", and in connection with which the province and the municipality must be prepared to become partners with the federal government. But in a matter like this surely the government ought to reorientate itself, its attitude and its policies. Its approach ought to be altogether different.
This is something that is left to the decision of the provinces and the municipalities. No effort is made to select the areas where unemployment is most serious and to say to the governing authorities in those areas, "The unemployment population is thus and thus; this winter works program is capable of providing a given number of men with jobs, but this will not be sufficient. We would like to sit down with you"-the province and the municipality-"and ascertain what kind of steps may be taken to provide work"-in the case of Windsor for over 10,500; in the case of Cornwall for over 4,000; in the case of Peterborough for over 5,000 unemployed people.
But to think we are satisfying our responsibility by this program alone, in the face of this particular emergency, is really to demonstrate without any shadow of doubt that this government has no real unemployment policy at all. The minister began his statement by saying that this was one of a series of measures which the government had brought forward to resolve this problem of unemployment.
What are the other measures? The housing legislation is the only one to which the minister can refer as having any immediate potential value. He certainly cannot refer to the vocational guidance program, the act that he brought in the other day; he cannot refer to the Small Loans Act amendment that was brought in the other day; he certainly cannot refer to the productivity council, because on the basis of his own statement those are programs not designed to provide work in the short term.
What are these other measures of which this program is a part? The real fact is there are really no other measures. This government does not know what to do about this problem; that is the real fact. But it recognizes that it has to do something and it brings forward this program only as a result of

Supply-Labour
prodding on the part of those who sit particularly in this part of the house. Only because of this prodding have we been able to get any kind of program in this particular at all.
The minister predicted on October 19 that the work approved under the government's winter works program would provide 17,894 jobs. The Minister of Trade and Commerce, who is not as conservative as the Minister of Labour, when speaking on September 22 said he was confident that the winter works program would put 200,000 people to work in Canada. That is a very different figure.
Would you repeat what I said about how many jobs it would provide.

I will read from the article in the Toronto Star. This is dated October 19 and reads:
Ottawa-The government has approved 964 municipal winter works projects for this year's incentive program, labour minister Starr said yesterday.
The federal government will pay $7 million of the total $58 million costs of these projects. Ottawa pays one half direct payroll costs.
The winter works program started Monday-six weeks earlier than last year-and will run to April 30.
Ontario has more than half-467-of the projects that were approved. British Columbia follows with 143 and Saskatchewan with 101.
Mr. Starr predicted the work approved will result in 17,894 jobs for a total of-
That was up to date; that was not for the whole winter.

The article continues:
Mr. Starr predicted the work approved will result in 17,894 jobs for a total of 970,160 man days of work.
I take it that the minister agrees that I have correctly quoted what he said.
No. The hon. member for Essex East left the impression that I said this municipal winter works program will only provide jobs for 17,000.
I did not say that.

What was reported in that newspaper was that on that date, a week after the project started on October 15, already 17,000 jobs were provided. But I did say we estimated that later on-not at that particular time, because I only gave the facts up to the receipt of the applications, which was only a week after the starting date-and I said again today, that the municipal winter works program would provide on-site jobs for 100,000 men. And the Minister of Trade and Commerce was quite correct.

There is no quarrel with the minister. What I said was that on October 19, 1960 the Minister of Labour

predicted that the work approved under the government's winter works program would provide 17,894 jobs, and that earlier the Minister of Trade and Commerce, on September 22, was reported to have said he was confident that 200,000 jobs would be created this winter by the extended winter works program.
He was right.
Quite correct.

On September 13, 1960 the Minister of Public Works was quoted as saying that it is uneconomic to construct public buildings to fight unemployment. This government really does not know what it should do. One minister says one thing and another minister says another. That causes the government whip to rise in his seat.
Mr. Pallet!: Would the hon. member say from whence the Minister of Public Works is quoted.

Yes, I will be very glad to do so. On September 13 in the Toronto Star we have the following:
Public works poor way to make jobs: Walker.
Federal public works minister David J. Walker said last night it is uneconomical to construct public buildings to fight unemployment.
"We can only justify the expense of any such building if Canada needs it," he said. Public works for the sake of providing jobs he termed "one of the most expensive ways" of creating employment.
And so on. I hope that satisfies the government whip.

Speaking to the ward two businessmen's association, of which he is honorary president-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

Speaking to the ward two businessmen's association, of which he is honorary president, Mr. Walker claimed the real solution to the employment problem lies with individual Canadians.
That is not what the Prime Minister said and that is not what the Minister of Labour said. He said only 15 per cent of last year's gross national product of almost $36 billion was created by government expenditure.

Another feature of this program is that the Minister of Labour speaks as though this particular program, to the extent that it is capable of providing some work, is a program about which the federal government has the right to claim full authorship. One is given the impression that it is a program the implementation of which is made possible entirely by the federal government. Oh.

In other words at that time the total cost of the program was $58 million and the federal share was only $7 million.
