speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Essex East has the floor.

Is it unreasonable to ask the government to seek to deal with this problem in a practical and more comprehensive manner? We have not had at any time from the Minister of Labour a breakdown of the categories of unemployed people. We have never had the minister tell us how many unemployed came from agriculture, forestry, fishing and trapping, mining and quarrying, manufacturing, construction, transportation, public utilities, trade, finance, insurance and services generally. We have never had in this committee since this government came into office a break-down of the categories of unemployed in our country.
I say that we cannot possibly deal adequately and comprehensively with this problem unless we know the full nature of the problem. We do not know whether it is cyclical or structural or a combination of both. We do not know the extent of seasonality in the problem. Either the minister does not have that information at his disposal or if he does he is reluctant for some reason or another to give it to the committee.
Since the fall of 1958 we have been urging that parliament be given this information. We have argued that if the minister does not have this information then this house should constitute itself into a committee for the purpose of obtaining from the experts in the government service and outside an assessment of the problem so that, having an assessment of it, we would be in a better position to know what to do about the problem. That is now being done in another place. It is a reflection on this government that it has denied to this house the right to elicit that kind of information when it was being made available and1 now, only at the end of the third year, it is being given to hon. gentlemen who are not the elected representatives of the people.
I say this government made a mistake at the outset, first of all in gambling on the risk, in failing to take the necessary steps to make an assessment of what the problem was. Had the government done that then it could act more effectively on the suggestion made tonight by the hon. member for Laurier. That is being done in the United States.
Under the Eugene McCarthy commission every major distressed area in the United States has been examined. The commission, appointed by congress for that purpose, has gone in and made a careful study of the situation in areas like Detroit, Chicago, Los Angeles and other communities in the United

Supply-Labour
States. There is now available for any student of the problem a careful portrayal of the nature of unemployment, broken down into the categories of the various occupations which I mentioned a moment ago.
We do not even have that in this country. If we have the Minister of Labour has never brought it forward. This is what we should have. This government at this late date should send in teams of assessment into Cornwall, Peterborough, Windsor, Toronto, Vancouver, Hamilton, Brantford and other areas where there are these heavy pockets of unemployment to ascertain precisely what is the nature of the problem of unemployment, and having determined that then take steps, in accordance with the government's policies and judgment, designed to deal with this problem in a comprehensive way.
The government has come forward and said that it has a program that will put more men to work this year. The minister said 100,000. What guarantee have we that a great percentage of that 100,000-if that is the correct figure-would not have been put to work under projects conceived, originated and maintained by the municipalities themselves or in conjunction with the governments of the provinces of which they are a part?
This particular program is good as far as it goes. It does not go far enough. It will not put enough people to work. It is a further indication of the complete bankruptcy of ideas of which this government day by day increasingly gives evidence.

Mr. Chairman, when I look upon the senatorial physique of the hon. member for Essex East and listen to his rollicking and rolling eloquence, I pay tribute to his impressive ability to make a verbal skirmish on economic injustice and unemployment sound like a major battle against evil. May I call it ten o'clock?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the house leader give some indication of what we will do tomorrow and from now until the recess?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Tomorrow, Mr. Speaker, I hope we will complete the supplementary estimates. There is the intervention of the private members' hour on Tuesday at five o'clock, so the time tomorrow afternoon is not very great. If the supplementary estimates are completed quickly I think the sensible thing to do would be to follow the suggestion made last Friday. We might take up some of the special committees to which I have drawn attention on several occasions, the ones with regard to procedure, Indian affairs and research.
On Tuesday evening the budget speech will be presented. Wednesday there will be a continuation of the debate on the budget and the house will recess at six o'clock, I presume.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Has the house leader given any consideration to introducing before Christmas his legislation concerning veterans?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I had hoped to do that, Mr. Speaker. As a matter of fact the resolution was introduced one week ago on Monday night but the balance of the week was spent on a lengthy debate on the productivity council and we were not able to deal with that resolution again. Time has now run out on us. My hope was that we would complete the resolution stage, have second reading and refer it to the standing committee but obviously there is now no opportunity before the recess to give to this resolution the full attention it deserves. It is very important legislation.
It being four minutes after ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
The following answer, deposited with the Clerk of the house, is printed in the official report of debates pursuant to standing order 39:

1.	Since January 1, 1960, has the Minister of Transport had any meetings with other members of parliament regarding the question of a coastguard1?
2.	If so: (a) upon what dates were such meetings held? (b) who was in attendance?
Answer by: Hon. Leon Balcer (Minister of
Transport):
1. and 2. No, but the former minister of transport has made himself available at different times to meet with members of parliament who had indicated their desire to discuss with him the matter of search and rescue service. There is no official record of when such meetings with members may have taken place, or of those who were present, so that the correct official reply is that the detailed information requested is not available.
